challenges.title: Who's It?

spec.goal: Turn the ear till each 'it' hears who it means. Then ring!

turnSpeed.unit: degrees per second while ← or → is held; speed ramps linearly from start to max over rampSeconds of holding

spec.roundsNote: Pool of 10. Each try deals them in a fresh seeded shuffle, never repeating within a try (a try needs at most 8). words: the sentence, in order. ask: index of the glowing word ('it'). means: index of the word 'it' really means. decoy: the other noun. Internal only: never show means or decoy.

keyLayout.rule: Every word of the round has a KEY: a flag at angle phi on the dial ring (degrees, 0 = up, clockwise). Per round: T = random 0..359. means gets phi = T. decoy gets T + 45 or T - 45 (random side). The other 7 words (both 'the's, the verb, 'because', 'it' itself, 'was', the last word) are shuffled into T+90, T+120, T+150, T+180, T+210, T+240, T+270.
keyLayout.why: Word order and flag order differ on purpose: the ear finds words by their key, not by where they stand. Aiming exactly at the right flag gives it about 95% of the pie; aiming between it and the decoy splits about 50/50 (a muddle); the 60% bar leaves a window about 62 degrees wide around the right flag.
keyLayout.startAim: The ear starts each round at T + 180 plus a random -60..+60 degrees, so every round needs a turn.

spin.note: From the 4th round of a try, the whole flag ring drifts slowly (direction alternates per round): the Fair wind. Rounds 1-3 stand still.

spec.math: q = (sin theta, -cos theta) for the ear angle theta; k_j = (sin phi_j, -cos phi_j). score_j = sharpness * dot(q, k_j) = sharpness * cos(theta - phi_j). w_j = exp(score_j - max score) / sum_k exp(score_k - max score). Recompute every frame. Never display sharpness, scores or the formula.

ring.good: argmax w === means AND w[means] >= threshold. Then: ding, ★ +1, the meant word's card hops, the 'it' card flips to show that word in its colour with a '!' (spec.feedback.good), a little confetti, next round after nextRoundDelay.
ring.muddle: anything else. Then: buzz, ✕ +1, the 'it' card wobbles and shows spec.feedback.muddle built from the two biggest slices (bigger first), or spec.feedback.wrong if the biggest slice is >= 0.85. Never show which word was right. Next round after nextRoundDelay + 0.3 s.
ring.slow: the round fuse burns out without a ring: counts as a muddle; the 'it' card shows spec.feedback.slow.

spec.lose: ✕ reaches maxMuddles -> 'lose'; the clock running out -> timeUp returns 'lose'.

layout.sentence: Top strip, centred at y = 88: one cut-paper word card per word (Fredoka 24 px, padding 12 px, gap 8 px). Each card's paper brightens with its live weight w_j (pale at 0, full colour at 1), so the whole sentence shows who is being heard. The 'it' card is pink #ff7ab8, lifted, with a '?' bubble ringed by the round fuse (a shrinking arc).
layout.dial: Left-centre, centre (320, 330), ring radius 160: a round cream paper dial. Each flag is a pin on the ring with a paper pill showing its word, in its colour; neighbours alternate label radius 160 / 188 so labels never overlap. In the middle sits the teal ear-trumpet (#3ec7b5), its bell pointing at theta, with a faint listening cone (+-12 degrees, decoration only).
layout.pie: Right, centre (740, 300), radius 92: the listening pie. One slice per word, in word colours, in sentence order, always a whole pie. Slices >= 8% carry their word. When the biggest slice reaches the threshold it lifts out with an ink outline (it shows 'focused', never 'correct').
layout.bubble: Under the pie at (740, 450): '{ask word} = {word of the biggest slice}' in that word's colour; the runner-up follows in small type when its slice is > 15%. This is the blend of the values: what 'it' would turn into if you rang now.

spec.input: ← → (A/D) turn the ear. The mouse over the dial (never the sentence strip) sets where the ear should point; the ear turns there at up to mouseTurn degrees per second, so the pie sweeps through the words on its way. A press on the dial aims at its point and its release rings once the ear has arrived; Space/Enter rings at once (or on arrival, while the ear is still turning to the mouse). Keys take over from the mouse; a still mouse never aims.
spec.embodies: One ear = one attention head. The ear's direction is the query, each flag is a key, the card glow and pie are the softmax weights (one whole pie, shared by every word at once), and the bubble is the weighted blend of the values. Playing well = pointing the query at the right key so the attention gets sharp, like the paper's Figure 4 heads on 'its'.

challenges.design: Mario Party-style rush, 55 s. Each round shows a short sentence with a glowing 'it'. The player reads it, decides who 'it' really means, turns the teal ear on the dial to that word's flag (keys are scattered round the dial, not in sentence order), watches the listening pie and the glowing cards, and rings. 6 good rings win; 3 muddles or the clock lose. The 10 sentences come in pairs that differ by one word (hungry/yummy), so 'it' means a different word each time and only the meaning decides.
challenges.paperLink: Section 3.2 (an attention function maps a query and key-value pairs to a weighted sum of the values, weighted by query-key compatibility); Section 3.2.1 (dot products of the query with all keys, then a softmax gives the weights); Figure 4 (heads resolving the anaphora 'its', with very sharp attention).
intro: Psst! My practice ear. Wherever it points, it listens hardest.
Fair gossip is full of 'it'. Turn my ear so each 'it' hears who it means!
success: It works! It hears everyone a little, and the right one a LOT.
retry: Read the whole sentence first. Then turn the ear.

challenges.title: Long Questions

questions.question: The paper's two towers. How many identical floors does each one have?
right: Sssix. Tall. Like me, standing up.

questions.question: The Bell's eight ears share one word-coat. How wide is each ear's slice?
The paper's big model trained on eight GPUs. For how long?

challenges.paperLink: Q1: Section 3.1 (encoder and decoder are each a stack of N = 6 identical layers; Figure 1's Nx). Q2: Section 3.2.2 (h = 8 heads, d_k = d_v = d_model/h = 64 with d_model = 512). Q3: Abstract, Section 5.2 and Section 6.1 (the big model trained for 300,000 steps, 3.5 days, on eight P100 GPUs; the base model took 12 hours).
challenges.design: Three questions in the dialogue box, all right in one go. Lengthwise, who complains nobody ever asks him anything, finally gets to ask. Long things: tower height, slice width, training time. The answers are only in the paper (Cursed Book): the slice question gives neither 512 nor 64, and '12 hours' (the base model) is a fair decoy for the big one.
intro: Nobody ever asks me anything. Ssso I shall ask YOU. Three long questions.
From the paper. All three right in one go. Ssss.
wrong: Hiss! No. That's wrong-wise, not Lengthwise.
success: Ssssplendid! Nobody's ever answered me before.
retry: It's all in the book. Long sections. My favourite kind.

challenges.title: Ear Jobs

spec.goal: Ring word posts, watch the ears, tag them at Dabble's board
reminder: Ring a few word posts. Each ear always does its one job.
Then tag all four ears on my board. Right here.

posts.where: A straight row on the open main path right of the bridge: post i at x = 22.83 + 1.8*i, y = 0, z = 1.0 (i = 0..7, sentence order, left to right; the row ends at x 35.43). Seen from the row's held shot (x 29.1), the c2 lantern (x 26, z 2.9) falls in the gap between 'bunny' and 'gave'. Clear of the tree at (25, -2.1), the well at (31, -1.3), the front fence (x 31.8..38.2, z 2.75..3.35), both lanterns, the pier ramp (x 21..23 from z 3.25) and every villager; the Speck passes in front of and behind the row. Check world.colliders once and nudge a post sideways if it overlaps.
posts.look: A cut-paper word card (0.95 wide, 0.5 tall, cream #fffdf6 with an ink back plate) on a thin wooden stick, card centre at y = 2.0 (above the Speck's head, so a Speck standing at a post never hides its card), the word in ink. A tiny brass hand-bell (#ffd35a) on top. The row pops up (scale-in) when the puzzle starts.
posts.collider: circle r = 0.3 at each post (w.addCollider; removed on destroy)
posts.interactable: label "Ring '{word}'" (for '.' use "Ring the full stop"), icon 🔔, radius 1.3, promptHeight 3.0 (above the bell). onInteract is instant: no dialogue.
posts.onRing: sfx('ding'), the little bell wiggles, the previous strings vanish, four tiny ear-trumpets (the board's trumpet, scaled 0.6, in the ears' colours) hop onto the rung card's top edge at the four ear spots, and each ear's strings zip out of its trumpet's mouth (0.3 s); they stay until another post is rung.

attention.rule: When post i (the query word) is rung, each ear has weights over the 8 posts (the keys).
attention.back: 0.85 on post i-1 (on post 0 itself when i = 0), the other 0.15 shared evenly by the other 7 posts.
attention.giver: 0.85 on post 1 'bunny' (on itself when i = 1), rest shared evenly.
attention.stop: 0.85 on post 7 '.' (on itself when i = 7), rest shared evenly.
attention.little: If word i is a little word (posts 0 'the', 3 'the', 5 'a'): 0.85 on post i+1 (bunny, frog, pie), rest shared evenly. Any other word: an even 1/8 on all eight posts (this ear has nothing to find).

strings.draw: For each ear, a string from the top of post i to the top of every post j with weight >= 0.1. Weight >= 0.5: a thick paper string (tube radius 0.06) in the ear's colour. Weight 0.1..0.5: a thin string (radius 0.024, opacity 0.6; any thinner or fainter vanishes at the game's camera distance). So the even 1/8 fan shows as eight thin strings: 'teal shrugs'.
strings.shape: Quadratic arc from ear k's trumpet mouth on post i to its spot on post j's card top (x offsets -0.37, -0.17, 0.17, 0.37; the bell sits in the middle), apex 0.8 + 0.35*|i-j| + 0.13*k above the card tops, bulging (k - 1.5)*0.18 in z, so arcs to the same post stay side by side on screen. j = i: a small loop above the post. The trumpets lean outward (0.34, 0.14, -0.14, -0.34 rad), so the four mouths stay apart.
strings.dots: Each post also gets a small dot in an ear's colour on its card while that ear listens to it most, so overlapping arcs stay readable.

board.where: Dabble's Fair board: on the front bank's back edge at x = 16.9, y = -0.95, z = 7.2, right beside Dabble (bank-left), facing the camera; collider: a rect as wide as the board, z 7.0..7.38, so the lane in front stays open between Dabble and the pier ramp (x 21..23). (The bank is only 2.1 deep: a board in its middle leaves only ~0.2-wide squeezes on the way from the pier to Dabble, and tall foreground grass hides x 18..19.5 from the camera.) The puzzle ends here, so the artefact appears by Dabble, as the story's resolution says.
board.look: A cream paper board (2.0 x 1.6) on two legs, header 'FAIR PROGRAM'; four small paper ear-trumpets pinned down its left side in the ears' colours (pink, sky, gold, teal, top to bottom), each with a blank paper tag beside it that shows the chosen tag label once set (on two lines when long).
board.interactable: label 'Fair board', icon 📋, radius 1.6, centred on the board's right half (x + 0.4, z + 0.35) so standing at the board never picks Dabble next door. Test hook: give it boardOf: 'e1'; give each post interactable postIndex: i (two posts are both 'the').
board.flow: Press E: the Speck steps beside the board, the camera closes in, then four questions in a row with w.ask('{icon} {name}'s job?', [the 7 tag labels in spec.tags order, 'Later'], { speaker: w.speakerOf('dabble'), neutral: true }): '💗 Pink ear's job?', '💙 Blue ear's job?', '💛 Gold ear's job?', '💚 Green ear's job?'. While a question is open its trumpet on the board waggles and its tag breathes. 'Later' stops (choices so far stay on the tags; the camera goes back). After the fourth answer, check: all four right -> the tags flutter off the board, the camera turns to the row, every ear fires its strings from every post at once (1.8 s), w.confetti(80), the camera comes back, then api.onSolved(). Otherwise w.speak('dabble', spec.feedback.wrongOne or wrongMany with {n} = number of wrong tags). Never say which tag is wrong. Tags may repeat (it is simply wrong).

spec.deduction: Two rings already separate everything: ring 'gave' (pink and sky both go to 'bunny', gold to '.', teal fans out), then ring 'the' or 'a' (pink goes back or loops, sky stays on 'bunny', teal jumps to the next word). Ringing 'bunny' shows sky looping on itself. Internal only: never show this.

wrongOne: Quack. One tag's wrong. Which? Not my job.
wrongMany: Quack. {n} tags are wrong. I just deliver.

spec.destroy: Remove the posts, trumpets, strings, board, colliders and interactables, and release any camera shot it holds. Leaving the world restarts the puzzle with blank tags.
spec.embodies: Each ear is one attention head. Ringing a word shows that head's attention from that word (the query) to every word (the keys), drawn like the paper's coloured head plots. Nobody assigned the jobs: the heads learned them, and the player reads each job off the strings.
spec.camera: w.camera shots, all looking down 14 degrees like the follow camera. On start: a glance at the row as it pops up (0.9 s there, 1.6 s of game time), then back. On a ring: a held shot framing the whole row and its tallest arcs (distance from the screen's aspect, at least 15), released as soon as the Speck walks off the row (x outside the row +-1.7, z outside -2.2..3.4). At the board: the Speck steps beside it (x 18.45, z 7.7) and a close-up (distance 8+) puts the board in the top half of the screen while its questions are open. On a win: the tags fly, then the row's shot for the burst, then back.

challenges.design: Finale walk-around. After the intro, the camera glances at the Sentence popping up as eight word posts past the bridge, and a 'FAIR PROGRAM' board with four blank ear tags stands by Dabble on the bank. Ring any post (E): four tiny ear-trumpets hop onto that word and shoot coloured strings to where each of the Bell's ears listens, and the camera frames the whole row. Each ear always does one job (one word back, who gave the pie, the full stop, little words find their pal). Ring a few posts, deduce the jobs, then tag the four ears at the board (close-up). All four right solves it; otherwise Dabble only says how many tags are wrong.
challenges.paperLink: Section 4, last paragraph (self-attention could yield more interpretable models; individual attention heads clearly learn to perform different tasks, many tied to the syntactic and semantic structure of sentences) and Figures 3-5 (attention from one word, one colour per head).
intro: Quack. The Fair program's printed. Except one bit: what each ear DOES.
Four ears lost their tags. I deliver programs. I don't write them.
Ring the word posts past the bridge. Watch the ears. Tag them on my board.
reminder: Ring a few word posts. Each ear always does its one job.
Then tag all four ears on my board. Right here.
locked: Quack. Post's late again. Every house, in order. By the last, the first note's crumpled.
My Fair program waits too: Bimble's ear and the long one's questions first. Then me!
success: Quack. All four right. The ears picked those jobs all by themselves?
Nobody taught them. Clever ears. Cleverer than roller skates, anyway.

guard: Do not say which word 'it' means in Bimble's practice-ear sentences or any sentence like them (the frog ate the pie / the duck dropped the note / the mouse fixed the Bell / the bunny threw the pie / the cat read the note, because it was hungry, yummy, torn, sleepy, broken, clever, burnt, grumpy, curious or short), and never say where to turn the ear or which flag to ring.

Do not say which job each coloured ear does on Dabble's FAIR PROGRAM board (pink: one word back; blue: who gave the pie; gold: the full stop; green: little words find their pal), and never confirm or correct a tag.
Do not give the number of identical layers in the encoder or decoder stack (N = 6, Section 3.1), and never pick or confirm an option of Lengthwise's tower question.
Do not state or compute the width of one attention head's slice, d_k = d_v = d_model / h = 64 (Section 3.2.2), for Lengthwise's slice question.
Do not say how long the big model trained (3.5 days on eight P100 GPUs; the base model took 12 hours), and never pick or confirm an option of Lengthwise's training-time question.
Never confirm or correct the player's answer to a quiz question, an ear tag or a practice-ear round in this region.

offlineHints.text: One ear asks; every word answers. Section 3.2 weighs them. Figure 4 hunts an 'its'.
Each head learns its own trade. The end of Section 4 says so; Figures 3 to 5 show them at work.
Count the floors where the towers are built: Section 3.1, and the N beside Figure 1.
Eight ears, one coat, cut evenly. Section 3.2.2 hands each ear its width.
Even the big one had to learn. The opening lines and Section 5.2 keep its calendar.
The long one measures towers, slices and time. Seek Sections 3.1 and 3.2.2, and the paper's opening lines.
